story: C. Michael Astle is a co-author of five Atlas papers from the Interventions Testing Program (ITP) of the US National Institute on Aging. The ITP tests drugs and supplements for effects on lifespan in genetically mixed mice, running the same experiment at three sites (The Jackson Laboratory, the University of Michigan and UT Health San Antonio) so that a result has to hold up in all three. The 2009 Nature paper (HAR2009) showed that rapamycin, a drug that blocks mTOR, extended lifespan even when started late in life at about 600 days of age. Later papers showed that the gain depends on dose and is larger in females (MIL2011, MIL2014), that acarbose and 17-alpha-estradiol extend life mainly in males (HAR2014), and that resveratrol, green tea extract, curcumin and several other popular compounds did not change lifespan (STR2012). Publishing negative results was part of the programme's design. All of this is mouse work.

Astle has worked with David Harrison at The Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, Maine, for decades. Their first joint PubMed paper, on immune-cell responses in mice, dates from 1976, and PubMed lists more than 50 papers by the two together. Their most recent joint paper in PubMed, from 2019, reported that adding glycine to the diet modestly extended lifespan in ITP mice. On that paper the name appears in full as C Michael Astle, at The Jackson Laboratory.

story: Calorie restriction, eating less without malnutrition, slows aging in many animals and lowers mTOR activity. CALERIE (Comprehensive Assessment of Long-term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy) was the first long trial to test it in healthy, non-obese people. William Kraus is last author of the 2016 report on its safety (ROM2016). Over two years, participants aimed to eat 25% fewer calories. The diet was safe overall, with no rise in serious problems, but bone density fell more than in the control group, so bone health needs watching in anyone who tries long-term restriction.

Kraus's PubMed record runs to hundreds of papers from Duke on exercise, heart and metabolic health. In 2026 Kraus is listed at the Duke Molecular Physiology Institute and the Division of Cardiology, for example on a follow-up of STRRIDE, a supervised exercise trial in older adults, which found that step counts from wearable devices tracked fitness and heart-health measures better than people's own reports of how much they exercised.

story: Jukka Hakkola is the senior author of LASSILA2026, a study that joins a small clinical trial with mouse work. The pregnane X receptor (PXR) is a protein in liver cells that detects many drugs and chemicals and switches on genes to deal with them. Rifampicin, an antibiotic, activates it strongly. In 16 healthy volunteers, one week of rifampicin made the liver about 2.7 percent larger relative to body weight. In male mice, activating PXR also enlarged the liver, and this came with higher activity of the AKT-MTOR growth pathway but not of YAP, another known driver of liver growth. The human part shows the effect is real in people, while the mTOR link comes from the mice.

Hakkola has worked on PXR for many years. PubMed lists him on more than 25 PXR papers from the University of Oulu, usually as senior author. A 2025 study from the group, for example, found Lasp2, a small cell-adhesion protein, as a new PXR target gene in mouse liver, with partners at Charles University in Hradec Kralove, Czech Republic. The wider theme is how drug-sensing receptors in the liver also change glucose and fat metabolism and the size of the organ.

He leads the pharmacology and toxicology group in the Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine at the University of Oulu, which is linked with Biocenter Oulu and Oulu University Hospital. His academic title and training could not be confirmed from an official page.

story: Multiple sclerosis is a disease in which the immune system attacks the fatty myelin sheath around nerve fibres. In a 2026 review in Immunologic Research, with Manoj Tongra as senior author, the authors map how two signalling routes interact in this disease: the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, which steers cell growth and the activity of immune cells, and the JAK/STAT pathway, which carries signals from inflammatory messengers called cytokines. They argue that drugs acting on both routes could reduce immune damage and loss of myelin. A review collects and interprets earlier work; it does not test this idea.

PubMed lists Tongra as Chief Scientific Officer of Celagenex Research in Thane, Mumbai. All of Tongra's papers found on PubMed date from 2026. They include reviews on how muscarinic and histamine receptor signals converge on PI3K/Akt/mTOR, on pentadecanoic acid as a possible mTOR modulator in age-related female infertility, and on growth-factor and immune signalling in autism, as well as rodent studies testing sulforaphane, a compound from broccoli, in models of multiple sclerosis-like and ALS-like nerve damage. Earlier training and career details could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Decoding the PI3K/Akt/mTOR-JAK/STAT signaling axis in multiple sclerosis: mechanistic crosstalk and therapeutic opportunities.

story: Qiangsun Zheng is the senior author of the Atlas study JIN2026B. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular rhythm of the heart's upper chambers, becomes much more common with age. The team aged mice quickly with D-galactose injections and fed some of them rapamycin. Rapamycin lowered the animals' susceptibility to atrial fibrillation and eased the structural and electrical remodelling of the atria. It also improved mitochondrial function and insulin sensitivity. The authors traced the effect mainly to lower activity of HIF-1 alpha, a protein that switches cell metabolism under low oxygen, and described it as independent of mTOR. The evidence comes from one mouse aging model.

Zheng leads a cardiology group that works closely with Xinghua Qin's laboratory at Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xi'an. Their mouse studies treat atrial fibrillation as partly a metabolic disease: a molecule released during exercise (BAIBA) protected obese mice through the energy sensor AMPK (2024), excess succinate raised the risk by harming mitochondria (2025), branched-chain amino acids raised it and swimming lowered it (2025), and very intense exercise raised it through over-active autophagy (2025). The group also studies reperfusion injury after heart attack.

On the clinical side, Zheng's recent papers look for blood markers that predict outcomes, such as an inflammation and nutrition score that forecast whether atrial fibrillation returns after catheter ablation (2026) and inflammation-related proteins in acute coronary syndrome (2026).

studies.title: Rapamycin attenuates age-related atrial remodeling and fibrillation by targeting HIF-1α-mediated metabolic dysregulation.

story: Do Jin Kim is a co-author of three Berkeley papers in this Atlas that describe, in atomic detail, the docking station for mTORC1, the growth-control complex, on the lysosome. SUX2017 combined several structural methods into a 'hybrid' model of the RagA/C-Ragulator complex, the scaffold that holds the Rag GTPases on the lysosome surface. LAW2018 found that nutrients change how tightly the Rag GTPases bind their lysosomal scaffold, Ragulator, a switch that controls whether mTORC1 is pulled to the lysosome. LAW2019 solved the structure of the folliculin complex, FLCN with its partner FNIP2, bound to the Rag GTPases and Ragulator on the lysosome. Folliculin acts as a checkpoint that switches on one of the Rag proteins, RagC, which mTORC1 needs to be recruited. Loss of FLCN causes Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an inherited condition with kidney tumours.
Structures like these explain how a nutrient signal is turned into a physical change in proteins, and they show where drugs might act. They come from purified proteins and cells, not from animals.

Kim's earlier papers with Hurley's group, from 2014 and 2015, mapped the protein complexes that start autophagy: the Atg1/ULK1 complex, the autophagy PI3-kinase complex and the Atg13-Atg101 pair. No current position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

story: In Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, faults in the FLCN gene cause skin bumps, lung cysts and kidney tumours. Wei-Ying Chen was the last author, usually the senior author, of the 2026 review CAO2026 in Frontiers in Oncology. The review argues against the old idea that FLCN loss simply turns on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, everywhere. FLCN works on the RagC/D switch proteins, which steer only some mTORC1 targets, especially the MiT/TFE transcription factors. Losing both FLCN copies lets these factors build up in the nucleus and drives kidney tumours, while one lost copy may be enough for lung and skin problems. It is a review of existing work, not a new experiment.

PubMed lists Chen in the Department of Urology of Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, affiliated to Wenzhou Medical University, on papers from 2023 to 2026. Together with Zhi-Lie Cao and Xiao-Ping Qi, Chen has co-authored case reports and reviews on rare hereditary tumours, such as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A, a pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma syndrome now called multiple endocrine neoplasia type 5 (2024), and a primary seminoma of the prostate (2023). story: Marion Horsch is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Horsch is listed at the Institute of Experimental Genetics and German Mouse Clinic in Neuherberg, near Munich, and PubMed shows more than fifty papers shared with Johannes Beckers, whose group measures which genes are switched on in mouse tissues. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. story: Taras Stasyk is a co-author of two Atlas studies about mTORC1 control at the lysosome. REB2015 (cells) found that SLC38A9, a transporter in the lysosome membrane, is part of the machinery that senses amino acids and passes the signal to mTORC1. NAP2020 (cells and mice) showed that mTORC1 reaches the transcription factor TFEB by a special route that needs RagC and RagD, and that this route drives kidney disease in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. Stasyk is in the middle of the author list on both.

story: Yu Chi Yang is a co-author of two Atlas papers on a new kind of mTOR drug. Rapamycin and its relatives only partly block mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and leave one of its key targets, 4E-BP1, largely untouched. Drugs that block the mTOR enzyme site block mTORC1 fully but also hit mTORC2, which causes side effects such as high blood sugar. Revolution Medicines built bi-steric molecules, which join a rapamycin-like part to an enzyme-site part so that they bind two places at once and prefer mTORC1. MEN2023 showed that one of them, RMC-6272, fully shut down mTORC1, including 4E-BP1, and overcame resistance to hormone therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer cells and in tumours from patients grown in mice. SCH2025 was the first trial of the related drug RMC-5552 in 57 patients with advanced solid tumours. High blood sugar was uncommon (4 percent) and the disease was controlled in 64 percent of patients, but with no comparison group the trial cannot prove that sparing mTORC2 is the reason.
PubMed lists Yang at Revolution Medicines in Redwood City, California, on 17 papers from 2023 to 2026, in the company's work on targeted cancer drugs.

story: Kathleen Ottina is a co-author on two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's lab. HSU2011 asked which proteins in a cell carry phosphate tags that depend on mTOR, the growth kinase. The team found that Grb10 is one of the proteins mTORC1 phosphorylates, and that Grb10 then damps signalling from insulin and growth factors through PI3K. This is a feedback loop: active mTORC1 turns down the signals that switch it on. The work was done in cultured cells.

BAR2013 found the off switch for the amino acid signal to mTORC1. A complex the lab named GATOR1 acts as a GAP for the Rag GTPases, a helper that makes these switch proteins turn themselves off when amino acids run low, while a second complex, GATOR2, opposes it. Some cancers carry mutations in GATOR1 genes; in those cell lines mTORC1 stayed on during amino acid starvation and the cells were very sensitive to rapamycin.

PubMed lists Ottina on two more papers from the same lab: a 2011 Genome Research RNAi screen for regulators of TORC1-S6K signalling in fruit-fly cells, and a 2014 Science Signaling study with Kris Wood's lab at Duke University that screened pathway-activating genes for those that let cancer cells survive targeted drugs, pointing to Notch1 in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer. There Ottina is listed at the Whitehead Institute and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the MIT Department of Biology. A current position could not be confirmed.

story: Douglas Covey is a co-author of two Atlas studies from the Zoncu lab on how lysosomes tell mTORC1, the growth-control complex, that cholesterol is available. In CAS2017 the team showed that cholesterol in the lysosome membrane switches on mTORC1. The transporter SLC38A9 is needed for this through cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein, separate from its role in sensing arginine, while NPC1, the protein that exports cholesterol out of the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. In SHI2022 they found a second sensor, LYCHOS (formerly called GPR155). When cholesterol is high, LYCHOS binds GATOR1, a brake on mTORC1, and takes it out of action, so mTORC1 can be recruited to the lysosome. Both studies were done mainly in cultured cells.

Covey's own field is the chemistry of steroids and sterols. Covey's group at Washington University makes modified versions of these molecules and tests how small changes in shape alter what they do. Much of this work, often with Mennerick, concerns neurosteroids, natural brain steroids that act on GABA-A receptors, the main inhibitory receptors of the brain, and their potential for treating psychiatric disorders. Recent papers use machine learning and screening to find new neurosteroid targets (2025), test steroid and sterol analogues on inflammation in brain immune cells (2026) and show that flipping the orientation of one hydroxy group in cholesterol changes how the molecule moves inside cells (2026).
PubMed lists Covey at the Department of Developmental Biology and the Taylor Family Institute for Innovative Psychiatric Research at Washington University School of Medicine.

story: Oliver Davis is a co-author of two Zoncu lab papers in this Atlas on cholesterol and mTORC1. Every cell has to decide whether it has enough raw materials to grow. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, makes that decision on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, where it is switched on when nutrients are present. Amino acids were the best-known signal; CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is another one. SLC38A9, a transporter-like protein already known to sense the amino acid arginine, is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and it uses separate cholesterol-responsive parts of the protein to do it. NPC1, the protein that moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, binds SLC38A9 and holds mTORC1 back. The experiments used cell lines and fibroblasts from patients, not whole animals. SHI2022 then found the cholesterol sensor itself: LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein previously known only as GPR155. Cholesterol binds one end of LYCHOS, and when cholesterol is high LYCHOS captures GATOR1, a complex that normally keeps mTORC1 off, which lets mTORC1 be recruited to the lysosome. This work was done in human cell lines and with purified proteins.

Davis followed this up as first author of a 2020 Developmental Cell paper titled 'NPC1-mTORC1 signaling couples cholesterol sensing to organelle homeostasis and is a targetable pathway in Niemann-Pick type C'. Niemann-Pick type C is a rare inherited disease in which cholesterol gets trapped in lysosomes and the brain and liver are damaged. The paper linked this cholesterol signal to the health of the cell's organelles and suggested that blocking mTORC1 could be a way to treat the disease. Davis was also second author of a 2019 Nature Cell Biology paper showing that contacts between the endoplasmic reticulum and the lysosome let mTORC1 sense cholesterol and drive abnormal growth signalling in the same disease.
No current position could be confirmed with certainty, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

story: Most breast cancers grow in response to the hormone estrogen, and hormone therapy is the main treatment. Over time many tumours stop responding, and part of that resistance runs through mTOR. BOLERO-2 (BAS2012) was a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 postmenopausal women whose hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer had progressed on an aromatase inhibitor. Adding the mTOR inhibitor everolimus to the hormone drug exemestane more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again, 10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review. The result led to approval of the combination. Mouth sores (stomatitis) were the main side effect. Michael Gnant was one of the co-authors.

The final overall-survival report (PIC2014) found a median of 31.0 months with everolimus plus exemestane and 26.6 months with placebo plus exemestane. That gap was not statistically significant, so the drug delayed progression but was not shown to lengthen life. Both papers are human trials.

Gnant is based at the Comprehensive Cancer Center of the Medical University of Vienna and at the Austrian Breast and Colorectal Cancer Study Group (ABCSG), the national trials group; the 2014 report gave the Department of Surgery as the address. PubMed lists close to 100 papers with Gnant, Vienna and ABCSG, many of them large breast cancer trials and treatment guidelines, such as a 2026 Austrian consensus on CDK4/6 inhibitors after surgery for early breast cancer.

story: Saeed A Hafez was first author of a 2026 Saudi Pharmaceutical Journal study (HAFEZ2026) on psoriasis, a common skin disease in which skin cells grow too fast and the skin becomes red, thick and scaly. The team produced a psoriasis-like rash in mice by rubbing imiquimod cream on the skin, a standard laboratory model. They then injected melittin, the main active peptide of bee venom. At the higher dose the rash score fell by about 60 percent.

The study links the effect to the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, the chain of signals that tells cells to grow. Melittin lowered the activity of this pathway in the skin and raised markers of autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system that mTOR normally holds back. This is one mouse model, with melittin given by injection into the abdomen, so it does not show that bee venom or melittin would help people with psoriasis.

PubMed lists Hafez at the Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, part of the Saudi Ministry of Health, in Abha. No other publication could be tied to this author with confidence, and a fuller career history could not be confirmed.

story: Tianxiong Xiao is first author of XIA2026, a review in Seminars in Cell and Developmental Biology. It does not report new experiments. It pulls together evidence that four nutrient-sensing systems, mTOR, AMPK, the sirtuins and insulin/IGF-1 signaling, work as one network to decide what adult stem cells do: stay at rest (quiescence), wake up and divide, or turn into specialised cells. Adult stem cells keep tissues such as blood, muscle, gut and brain supplied with new cells, so this decision matters throughout life.

The review argues that with age the network drifts out of balance, for example with mTOR too active, which can wear stem cells out and add to tissue decline. Because it is a review, its framework is a proposal built on mostly animal and cell studies, and the Atlas treats it as a map of ideas rather than as evidence in its own right.

PubMed lists Xiao at the Key Laboratory of Systems Health Science of Zhejiang Province, School of Life Science, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, with Hu C as senior author. No other papers could be tied to this person with confidence, and no profile page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one at the time of the study.

studies.title: Nutrient-sensing pathways in adult stem cells: Orchestrating homeostasis, aging, and disease

previous_note: Common surname; no further identity-confirmed papers. Career path unknown.

current.lab_name: School of Medicine, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (Nanjing, China)
current.role: Researcher at Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine who led a mouse study showing that the age-related loss of Lamtor5, a part of the lysosomal platform that helps switch on mTORC1, drives immune ageing through inflammation
current.sub: School of Medicine, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Nianyin Lv is the first author of LV2026. mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of lysosomes, with the help of a protein complex called the Ragulator (LAMTOR1 to LAMTOR5) that anchors the docking machinery there. The study found that one of these proteins, Lamtor5, falls with age in macrophages, the immune cells that eat debris and germs. When Lamtor5 is lost, macrophages age early and release signals through the cGAS-STING pathway, a DNA-sensing alarm system, that spread inflammation to other tissues and push the whole body toward ageing. Putting Lamtor5 back into old mice reversed the immune ageing and eased other ageing signs. The work is in mice and gives a link between lysosomes, mTOR signalling and inflammation in old age.

PubMed shows other papers under the same initials at Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine, but they could not be tied to this researcher with confidence, so they are not used here. No official profile was found, so training and current position are not given.

studies.title: Age-associated decline of Lamtor5 drives immunosenescence and systemic aging via cGAS-mediated paracrine inflammation.

previous_note: Common name; other Lv N papers (including an unrelated orthopaedic Lv Nanning) not attributed. Profile from the Atlas paper only.

current.lab_name: Centre for Computational and Systems Biology (COSBI), Fondazione The Microsoft Research - University of Trento (Rovereto, Italy)
current.role: Mathematical modeller in Trento who applies survival and epidemic models to medical data, and first author of the 2026 re-analysis of the RAP-ALS rapamycin trial in ALS
current.sub: COSBI, Fondazione The Microsoft Research - University of Trento (2026)
story: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disease in which the nerve cells that control muscles die. RAP-ALS was a small clinical trial of rapamycin, the drug that blocks the growth-control complex mTORC1, in people with ALS. In the Atlas study DEN2026B, De Nardi and colleagues went back to the trial data (63 patients) and asked which factors predicted survival. Among carriers of a mutation in the C9orf72 gene, the most common genetic cause of ALS, those treated with rapamycin survived longer, and the same pattern held against a separate group of 40 C9orf72 carriers.

This is a secondary, exploratory analysis. The number of treated C9orf72 carriers was small, and the patients were not randomised for this question, so the drug may not be the cause of the difference. The result is a reason for a proper trial in this genetic group, not evidence that rapamycin works in ALS.
PubMed lists De Nardi in 2026 at COSBI in Rovereto, a computational biology centre run jointly by Microsoft Research and the University of Trento.

studies.title: Multivariate Survival Analysis of a Comprehensive Clinical Trial of Rapamycin in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Explores Prognostic Factors and Survival Patterns in C9orf72 Carriers

current.lab_name: Oh Lab, Department of Biomedical Science and Engineering, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (Gwangju, South Korea)
current.role: Researcher in Chang-Myung Oh's lab at GIST who tested urolithin A, a gut-microbe product, in mice with a stiff-heart form of heart failure
current.sub: Department of Biomedical Science and Engineering, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (papers with Chang-Myung Oh)
story: Hangyul Song is the first author of SONH2026, a study in Experimental and Molecular Medicine from Chang-Myung Oh's lab at the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST) in South Korea. It deals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF): the heart still pumps out a normal share of its blood with each beat, but the muscle is stiff and thick and fills poorly. HFpEF is common in older people with obesity and diabetes and has few good treatments.

Urolithin A is made by gut bacteria from compounds in foods such as pomegranates and walnuts. In mice with HFpEF it eased heart stiffness, thickening and scarring. In heart cells it switched on AMPK, the energy sensor, and lowered mTOR activity. That restored mitophagy, the clearing of damaged mitochondria. Urolithin A also changed the gut microbiome and lowered ceramides, fatty molecules that harm heart cells. The results come from mice and cell models, not from patients.
PubMed lists several papers shared by Song and Oh. No separate profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Urolithin A activates mitophagy via the AMPK-mTOR axis and modulates the gut-ceramide axis to ameliorate cardiac remodeling in HFpEF

previous_note: No profile found; role (student or postdoc) not known.

current.lab_name: Xuefeng Yu group, Division of Endocrinology, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
current.role: Endocrinology researcher in Xuefeng Yu's group at Tongji Hospital in Wuhan who studies the liver- and fat-derived hormone ANGPTL8 in aging and diabetes
current.sub: Division of Endocrinology, Department of Internal Medicine, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (papers 2024–2026)
story: Yi He is first author of the Atlas study HE2026, with Xuefeng Yu as senior author. ANGPTL8 is a hormone-like protein released into the blood that helps control fat and sugar metabolism. In a large human cohort, higher ANGPTL8 levels went along with an older biological age and a higher risk of death. In mice, deleting the Angptl8 gene lengthened life and lowered markers of senescence, the state in which cells stop dividing and release inflammatory signals.

The team traced the mechanism in fat tissue. ANGPTL8 binds AKT2, a kinase in the insulin pathway, and drives the AKT-mTOR-S6K chain that pushes fat cells into senescence; blocking that chain removed the effect. The human data are associations, while cause and mechanism come from mice and cells, so ANGPTL8 is a candidate driver of fat-tissue aging rather than a proven one in people.

Yi He's other papers come from the same Tongji endocrinology group and follow ANGPTL8 into other organs: it steers bone marrow stem cells towards fat instead of bone during skeletal aging (2025), it drives inflammation and scarring in kidney tubule cells in diabetic kidney disease through AKT2 (2025), and blocking it protected against diabetes-related memory problems in mice (2024).

studies.title: An ANGPTL8-AKT2-mTOR Axis Drives Adipose Senescence and Aging-Related Functional Decline

current.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Hôpital Édouard Herriot, Hospices Civils de Lyon (Lyon, France)
current.role: Medical oncologist in Lyon who specialises in neuroendocrine tumours and led the COMPETE phase 3 trial comparing 177Lu-edotreotide with everolimus
current.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Hôpital Édouard Herriot, Lyon (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Neuroendocrine tumours of the gut and pancreas grow from hormone-making cells. Many carry receptors for the hormone somatostatin on their surface, which can be used to deliver radiation straight to the tumour: a somatostatin-like molecule is linked to a radioactive atom such as lutetium-177, an approach called peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. Everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, is a standard drug for these tumours. In WALTER2026, Thomas Walter was first author of COMPETE, a phase 3 randomised trial in 309 patients that compared 177Lu-edotreotide with everolimus. Median progression-free survival was 23.9 months with the radioligand and 14.1 months with everolimus, and serious treatment-related side effects were less common (18 percent against 40 percent). The trial was open-label, so patients and doctors knew which treatment was given. For the mTOR field, the result means an mTOR inhibitor was the comparator that a newer therapy beat in this disease.
Walter works in the Department of Medical Oncology at Hôpital Édouard Herriot in Lyon. PubMed lists more than 140 papers under this name on neuroendocrine tumours with Lyon affiliations.

studies.title: [177Lu]Lu-edotreotide versus everolimus for gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (COMPETE): a phase 3, multicentre, randomised, open-label, superiority trial.

current.lab_name: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (Aurora, Colorado, USA)
current.role: Obstetrician-scientist from Sapporo Medical University working in the Colorado placenta group of Thomas Jansson, Theresa Powell and Fredrick Rosario on how mTOR controls nutrient transport to the fetus
current.sub: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (2024–2026) · Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Sapporo Medical University
story: The placenta decides how much food reaches a growing baby, and mTORC1, the cell's nutrient and growth sensor, helps set how fast it pumps amino acids across. In the 2026 study led by Hiroshi Shimada, with Fredrick Rosario as senior author, the team compared 46 placentas from healthy term pregnancies. Placentas from boys showed stronger mTORC1 signalling, more System A amino acid transport and higher mitochondrial respiration than placentas from girls, and boys had a higher birth weight relative to placental weight.

This was a snapshot at one time point with no treatment, so it shows an association between fetal sex and placental function, not a cause. It does suggest that male and female pregnancies may need to be analysed separately in placental research.

Shimada is listed by PubMed with both the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and Sapporo Medical University in Japan. Earlier work in the Colorado group includes a 2024 review on how placental amino acid transporters are regulated, with mTOR as a key regulator, and a 2025 mouse study in which switching off mTOR only in placental trophoblast cells cut the transport of folate to the fetus and reduced fetal growth.

studies.title: Sexual Dimorphism in Placental mTORC1 Signaling, Amino Acid Transport, and Mitochondrial Respiration at Term.

current.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology, College of Pharmacy, Beihua University (Jilin, China)
current.role: Pharmacologist at Beihua University who studies how plant-derived compounds protect the kidney and heart from damage caused by high blood pressure in mice
current.sub: Department of Pharmacology, College of Pharmacy, Beihua University, Jilin (papers 2026)
story: High blood pressure slowly damages the kidney. In the Atlas study CUI2026 in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology, Xiaoli Cui was first author. Mice received angiotensin II, a hormone that raises blood pressure and injures the kidney. Treatment with forsythoside A, a compound from the medicinal plant Forsythia, protected the kidney. The team reports that forsythoside A binds a protein called ASCL1 and so blocks a downstream CCNB1/mTOR axis. With mTOR held back, the cells cleared more damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) and suffered less ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Blood pressure itself did not fall, so the protection came from inside the kidney cells. The work was done in mice and cells.

Cui works in the Department of Pharmacology of the College of Pharmacy at Beihua University in Jilin, China, with Mengyang Wang, the senior author of CUI2026. In 2026 the same group reported that fangchinoline, an alkaloid from the plant Stephania tetrandra, protected mouse hearts from angiotensin II-induced heart failure through mitophagy and less ferroptosis, and that schisandrin B eased fatty liver disease in mice through the receptor PPAR-gamma. No official profile page was found, so the career path before 2026 is not known.

studies.title: Forsythoside A Alleviates Hypertensive Nephropathy by Promoting Mitophagy and Inhibiting Ferroptosis via ASCL1-CCNB1/mTOR Pathway.

current.lab_name: Cappell Lab, Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
current.role: Cell cycle researcher in Steven Cappell's lab at the National Cancer Institute who found that mTOR briefly switches off the APC/C to give cells a burst of glycolysis as they start to divide
current.sub: Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (Steven Cappell lab, papers 2021–2025)
story: Debasish Paul is first author of PAU2025, a Nature paper about the moment a resting cell decides to divide. When a growth signal arrives, mTOR quickly adds a phosphate to CDH1, the helper protein of a large enzyme called APC/C that tags other proteins for destruction. This partly releases CDH1 and briefly switches APC/C off. One of APC/C's usual targets, the glycolysis enzyme PFKFB3, then builds up, and the cell burns more glucose for a while, until a slower-acting phosphatase turns APC/C back on. The study, in human cells, showed that this short pulse of glycolysis is needed for cells to enter the cell cycle.

The finding gives mTOR a new job: besides boosting protein synthesis, it times a metabolic switch by reaching into the cell-cycle machinery. Because many cancers have overactive mTOR, the circuit may also help explain how tumor cells keep their fuel supply high, although the paper itself did not test tumors.

The publication record places Paul in Steven Cappell's lab at the Center for Cancer Research of the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda from at least 2021, when the group published a study showing that cells hit by DNA damage early in the cycle often keep going rather than stopping at the classic checkpoint. The lab uses time-lapse imaging of single living cells to follow cell-cycle decisions. No profile page was found, so the current role is not confirmed.

studies.title: Transient APC/C inactivation by mTOR boosts glycolysis during cell cycle entry
